newsitem.title: ITALY: Olivetti, Consob to issue statement on Friday.
newsitem.headline: Olivetti, Consob to issue statement on Friday.

text.p: Italy's troubled hi-tech company Olivetti is set to issue a statement on Friday morning after the loss-making group met with stock market watchdog Consob on Thursday aimed at clarifying its financial accounts.

An Olivetti spokeswoman said after the three and a half hour meeting in Rome between Consob and Olivetti officials led by chief executive Francesco Caio that there would be a joint Olivetti-Consob communique issued on Friday morning.
During the meeting a Consob spokesman had told reporters that the statement would be released around 0700 GMT on Friday.

Earlier on Thursday, Consob met with Renzo Francesconi, a former Olivetti director-general who resigned on Wednesday after only six week at the company, when he expressed misgivings about the way Olivetti presented its first half 1996 results.
"We gave all the elements to Consob to show Francesconi's statements were groundless," Caio told reporters after the meeting with Consob had finished.
Olivetti shares were suspended on the Milan stock exchange ahead of the meetings called by Consob, and were likely to remain suspended until the statement on Friday morning.

This was the latest twist in a week of high drama which had seen Olivetti's stock price plunge and then stabilise after tycoon Carlo De Benedetti resigned as chairman on Tuesday, ending 18 years at the helm.

Caio, widely seen as having won out in a boardroom power struggle with De Benedetti, had been summoned to Rome by Consob along with De Benedetti's successor as chairman Antonio Tesone and other company officials.
Olivetti said on Thursday that Francesconi's comments were completely unfounded and that it had instructed lawyers "to take action in defence of the company's moral standing."
Olivetti, which has not made a profit since 1990, announced a pre-tax loss for the first six months of 1996 of 440.2 billion lire ($291 million).

Francesconi was quoted in newspapers on Thursday as saying after he announced he was standing down: "You can make compromises over strategic plans but you really can't do that with figures and the accounts."
Milan financial daily Il Sole 24 Ore said in a front page editorial that the implications of Francesconi's remarks were "very serious if they are authentic, irresponsible if false."
Equity analysts who took part in a conference call with Caio on Wednesday evening said he had evaded questions about the presentation of the half-yearly accounts.
"Caio was asked about it but did not say anything," said Angela Dean, European technology analyst at Morgan Stanley. "It's all rather confusing and it does not help build confidence."
An Italian share analyst who listened in on the call expressed alarm at the state of Olivetti's finances.

"I am very worried. I think the company is totally out of control. Caio talked for two hours and said practically nothing," said the analyst with a major Milan finance house who asked not to be identified.
Foreign institutional investors, who now own about 70 percent of Olivetti, have put strong pressure on the company to give more information about where it is heading.

Questions over the true state of Olivetti were likely to focus on the group's stricken personal computer interests. This has been a huge drain on cash in recent years and many industry observers believe Olivetti should cut its losses and get out of the business altogether before it drags down the entire group.
Olivetti is engaged in a painful transition from PCs, which made fat profits in the 1980s before plunging into the red, to telecommunications, widely seen as the moneymaker of the 1990s.
